content: Individuals diagnosed with serious mental illness are statistically more likely to smoke heavily and exhibit greater dependence on nicotine compared to the general population. This phenomenon may be attributed to several factors, including a shared underlying cause between smoking and the mental illness, the use of smoking as a form of self-medication, efforts to mitigate the adverse effects of psychiatric medications, environmental boredom, or a combination of these elements. Addressing this issue is critical to improving the health and safety of individuals with serious mental illness who smoke, while also reducing the financial and health-related burdens on both the individual and society at large. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of smoking cessation advice on individuals with serious mental illness. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Schizophrenia Group Specialized Trials Register up to April 2, 2015. This register is regularly updated with data from CENTRAL, BIOSIS, PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and various trial registries. Additionally, unsystematic searches were performed on a subset of databases, including BNI, CINAHL, EMBASE, MEDLINE, and PsycINFO, up to the same date. References from all identified studies were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria for this review specified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared smoking cessation advice with either standard care or other targeted methods of delivering care or information. However, after independently screening the search results, the review authors (PK, AC, and DB) did not identify any trials that met these criteria. No RCTs were found that specifically evaluated the effectiveness of smoking cessation advice for individuals with serious mental illness. Despite this, the excluded studies demonstrated that it is feasible to randomize care packages tailored to smokers with serious mental illness. In conclusion, individuals with serious mental illness are disproportionately affected by smoking compared to the general population. However, there is currently no high-quality evidence available to guide healthcare professionals in providing effective smoking cessation advice to this population. This represents a significant gap in the literature, highlighting the need for well-designed trials in this area.
